answer: Complete scientific evidence from 'Projecting long-term excess risks of major infectious diseases associated with future extreme weather events in Thailand' (Choo et al., 2026, PLOS Negl Trop Dis 20(1): e0013896).

statistical_model.model_type: Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) with Negative Binomial distribution
statistical_model.distribution_rationale: Overdispersed disease case count data based on Cameron and Trivedi tests
covariates: Lagged monthly number of extreme heat days
Calendar month smooths (thin-plate splines) for seasonality

disease_lag_structures.dengue_and_jev: 2–3 months lag (extrinsic incubation period & vector reproduction)
disease_lag_structures.malaria: 1 month heat lag / 3 months SPI lag (EIP vs habitat accumulation)
disease_lag_structures.pneumonia_influenza_leptospirosis: 3 months lag (cumulative weather impact on host immunity & exposure)
disease_lag_structures.melioidosis: Immediate heat lag / 3 months SPI lag (soil bacterium exposure dynamics)

historical_baseline_data.meteorological_baseline_period: 2003–2021 (ERA5 hourly reanalysis spatially averaged to provinces)
historical_baseline_data.extreme_heat_definition: Daily maximum temperature > 34.9°C (90th percentile national threshold) for ≥3 consecutive days
historical_baseline_data.drought_and_wetness_definition: SPI-1 ≤ -1.5 (extreme dry / drought) and SPI-1 ≥ 1.5 (extreme wet / heavy precipitation)

climate_change_scenarios_and_gcms.primary_gcm: MIROC6 (tailored for Asian monsoon systems and ocean-atmosphere interactions)

diseases_evaluated.historical_heat_association: Positive IRR under moderate extreme heat; negative under prolonged extreme dry/wet conditions
Positive IRR with extreme heat days
Negative IRR with extreme heat; positive IRR with extreme dry weather
Positive IRR under extreme heat (>8 days/month); negative during extreme wet weather
Negative IRR with extreme heat; positive IRR with extreme wet weather
Strong positive IRR under extreme heat (>20 days/month) and extreme wet weather

dengue_projections.ssp245_near_term_spike_2021_2040: +26.2% (95% CI: 0.90%, 51.7%) increase driven by moderate extreme heat

influenza_projections.ssp245_near_term_trend: Peaks in 2021–2060 under moderate warming driven by heat and dry spells
influenza_projections.late_century_trend: Declines due to increased heavy precipitation flushing/reduced social mixing

other_disease_trends.melioidosis: Steeply increases under extreme heat (+27.8% by 2100 under SSP585) and extreme wet weather (+25.4% in 2041–2060)
other_disease_trends.pneumonia: Sustained increase during extreme weather periods under SSP585
other_disease_trends.malaria: Increases during extreme dry weather across climate scenarios
other_disease_trends.leptospirosis_and_jev: General risk reduction during extreme dry/heat conditions

vector_borne_mechanisms.aedes_aegypti_eip: Moderate heat shortens the Extrinsic Incubation Period (EIP), accelerating viral replication and transmission in early century under SSP245
vector_borne_mechanisms.drought_disruption: Severe dry weather shrinks artificial and natural water containers, restricting egg-laying breeding sites
vector_borne_mechanisms.rain_flushing_effect: Extreme wet weather flushes out mosquito larvae and breeding containers
vector_borne_mechanisms.humidity_impact: Lower relative humidity reduces adult mosquito lifespan and oviposition rates, acting as a primary driver for late-century dengue decline

respiratory_mechanisms.heat_and_dehydration_stress: High ambient temperatures and dehydration weaken respiratory epithelial integrity and mucosal immunity, elevating influenza and pneumonia susceptibility
respiratory_mechanisms.social_mixing_reduction: Extreme rainfall suppresses human outdoor mobility, leading to reduced contact rates and lower respiratory transmission

bacterial_environmental_mechanisms.burkholderia_pseudomallei: Extreme heat accelerates bacterial multiplication in surface soil, while flooding and heavy rainfall disperse bacteria into surface water and air

section_5_policy_implications_and_nap_re.precision_public_health: Move away from uniform national public health planning toward province-specific early warning triggers reflecting regional climate heterogeneity

operational_triggers_under_ssp245.northern_and_central_thailand: Target Bangkok, Chiang Rai, and Central provinces with vector control and hospital surge capacity during heatwaves accompanied by normal rainfall
operational_triggers_under_ssp245.northeastern_thailand: Target Nakhon Ratchasima, Buri Ram, and Ubon Ratchathani with influenza vaccination drives and respiratory surveillance during heatwaves coupled with extended dry periods

integration_with_dcce_and_nap: Incorporate climate-disease risk maps directly into Thailand's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) health sector guidelines
Establish automated provincial warning thresholds combining 3-day temperature spikes (>34.9°C) and SPI drought/flood indices to allocate public health resources dynamically
